screens.title: The Pythonic Way: Syntax and Basic Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: You are transitioning from C to Python, and this shift is about expressing ideas with fewer low-level details. Python emphasizes readable layout: the structure of your code is visible in its indentation, so the way you space lines actually shapes program flow. That readability makes it easier to prototype solutions and collaborate. In this chapter you will learn how to write small Python programs using consistent indentation and comments, how variables receive types dynamically, and how the core data types — integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans — behave. You will also use the print function to show results and the input function to gather user text, remembering that input always returns a string and often needs conversion for numeric work. Finally, you will practice arithmetic, comparison and logical operators to make decisions and compute values. A short hands-on greeter ties these pieces together: ask for a name and birth year, convert types, compute an age, and print a formatted greeting. Keep an eye out for two common pitfalls: mixing tabs and spaces, and forgetting to convert input before doing math. How might those errors affect a simple greeter program you write?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › The Pythonic Way
The Pythonic Way: Syntax and Basic Data Types
Readable syntax, dynamic typing, and core types you will use every day.
In this lesson
Learn indentation, variables, and the four fundamental types. Practice input and output and basic operators so you can write small, correct programs quickly.
Why it matters
Readable code reduces bugs and speeds collaboration. Dynamic typing lets you iterate faster, but requires attention to conversions when handling user input.
Common pitfalls
Mixing tabs and spaces causes indentation errors. Forgetting to convert input before arithmetic causes type errors at runtime.
Hands-on
Build a greeter that asks for name, color, and birth year, converts the year to a number, computes age, and prints a personalized message.
Explore Key Topics
Indentation, core data types, and simple input/output are the essential pillars for writing beginner Python programs.
Concept map
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Indentation → defines blocks
Types → int, float, str, bool
I/O & Operators → print, input, arithmetic
Sample flow
Ask user for text, convert numbers when needed, compute results, and display with the print function. Watch for type mismatches and indentation errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice so you develop reliable beginner skills. First, you will understand Python's guiding philosophy of readability and simplicity. That means appreciating how indentation, clear naming, and concise constructs help you and others read code the same way. Second, you will write basic Python programs that use consistent indentation, useful comments, and simple variable assignment. This skill matters because correct indentation is required syntax in Python, not optional formatting. Third, you will identify and use the four fundamental data types: integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans. You will learn their essential properties — for example that strings are immutable and input always arrives as text. Fourth, you will perform input and output with the print function and the input function, and you will convert input strings into numbers when necessary to avoid runtime type errors. Practicing these four objectives gives you a foundation for composing larger programs and avoiding the most common beginner mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practice and avoiding common mistakes. First, you will apply arithmetic operators such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, true division and floor division, and exponentiation so you can compute values correctly. You will also practice comparison operators to form boolean expressions that drive decisions in your code. Second, you will learn logical operators — and, or, and not — to combine conditions safely. Third, you will practice safe type handling with dynamic typing: variables can change type at runtime, so you will learn patterns to avoid confusing reassignments and to keep code predictable. Fourth, you will diagnose two frequent runtime issues: forgetting to convert input strings to numbers before arithmetic, which raises type errors, and mixing tabs and spaces which raises indentation errors. Each objective will be practiced with a short code example so you can see the error and the correct fix immediately.

screens.title: Hello, World — C vs Python
screens.narratorSegment: A short side-by-side example makes the differences clear and actionable. In C, you declare a main function, include headers, and use explicit types and semicolons; the structure is delimited with braces. In Python, a simple print function and a line of text are often enough; no semicolons or explicit function wrapper is required for a top-level script. The key takeaway is that Python removes ceremony so you can express ideas faster, but it enforces structure through consistent indentation rather than braces. Try to read both examples aloud: notice how Python’s indentation shows scope directly, while C’s braces separate structural markers from the code body. A common misconception is to think Python doesn’t enforce structure — it does, via whitespace. Another is to assume Python lacks performance or control compared to C; different trade-offs exist but both are useful tools. Finally, practice converting small C snippets into Python: remove the type declarations and braces, keep the algorithm and logic, and rely on the interpreter to manage memory details for you. Hello, World — C vs Python means c uses explicit types, semicolons, and braces while python uses indentation and dynamic typing to express the same logic more concisely.. In practical terms, contrast syntax, explicit types, and the role of indentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hello, World — C vs Python
C example
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello, World!
");
    return 0;
}
C requires headers, a main function, explicit return, and braces to mark scope. Types and semicolons are explicit.
Python example
print("Hello, World!")
Python uses a single call to the print function. Scope is shown by indentation when defining blocks like functions or conditionals.
Example
Translate a small C function into Python by keeping the algorithm and removing explicit type declarations and braces.
Common mistake
Expecting braces or semicolons in Python. Indentation is mandatory and mixing tabs/spaces causes errors.
Takeaway
Focus on the algorithm and let Python handle low-level details; be deliberate about indentation and variable types.

screens.title: Indentation and Block Structure
screens.narratorSegment: Indentation in Python is not cosmetic — it determines program structure. Where other languages use braces to delimit a block of code, Python increases indentation to start a block and reduces it to end one. The conventional standard is four spaces per level. A frequent beginner error is mixing tabs and spaces: this can raise an indentation error that stops your program. To avoid this, configure your editor to insert spaces for tabs, and be consistent across the entire file. Consider a simple conditional: when a condition holds, the indented lines that follow are executed. If you accidentally align a line incorrectly, the interpreter will either treat it as outside the block or raise an error. A helpful mental model is thinking of indentation as a stack of nested scopes: each indentation level pushes a new scope, and dedenting pops it. Practice by reading samples and re-indenting with a consistent width; that practice will make reading and debugging faster. Finally, remember that comments do not affect indentation but must be aligned properly if they appear inside a block. Indentation and Block Structure means use consistent indentation (four spaces recommended); python uses indentation to mark blocks and mixing tabs with spaces causes syntax errors.. In practical terms, why whitespace defines control flow in python. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Indentation and Block Structure
Definition
Indentation defines which statements belong to which blocks, such as the body of an if statement or a loop. Use four spaces per level for consistency.
x = 10
if x > 5:
    print("x is greater than 5")
    print("still in the block")
print("outside the block")
Misplacing indentation changes which lines run conditionally and can introduce subtle bugs or raise IndentationError exceptions.
Practice tips
  • Set your editor to insert spaces, not tabs.
  • Use four spaces per indentation level as the community convention.
  • When copying code, re-indent to match your file’s style.
Common mistake
Mixing tabs and spaces leads to hard-to-find errors. Reformatting in your editor fixes many indentation problems.
Key takeaway
Indentation is syntax. Be consistent and your code will be both valid and easier to read.

screens.title: Comments, Variables, and Dynamic Typing
screens.narratorSegment: Comments are written with the hash symbol and anything after that symbol on a line is ignored by the interpreter; use them to explain intent, not restate the code. Variable assignment in Python does not declare a type explicitly — the interpreter infers a variable’s type from its value when you assign it. For example, assigning ten sets the variable to an integer; later assigning a string replaces that value and type. This flexibility is powerful for quick experimentation but can also hide bugs if you accidentally reuse a name for a different kind of value. A concrete pattern is to keep variable names descriptive and consistent in use: use a name as a number holder or a text holder, not both. In the code panel you will see examples that show assignment, comments, and a reassignment that changes type. Notice the recommended habit: avoid reassigning wildly different types to the same name in a single scope. Also, prefer short comments that explain why a block exists rather than what each line does. Comments, Variables, and Dynamic Typing means use clear names and consistent uses for variables; dynamic typing helps speed development but requires disciplined naming to avoid confusion.. In practical terms, how to name values and what dynamic typing means in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Comments, Variables, and Dynamic Typing
Code examples
# Ask for a name and store it as text
name = input("What is your name? ")  # user's name as a string

# Assign a number
x = 10

# Reassigning to a different type is allowed but can be confusing
x = "ten"  # now x holds text, not a number

print(name)
print(x)
Comments explain intent. Variable names are your contract with future readers; changing a variable’s role can break that contract.
Explanation & analogy
Think of a variable name as a labeled jar. In Python you can replace the contents with any type of item, but if you swap contents frequently you confuse anyone who expects the jar to hold one thing.
Pro tip
Use descriptive names and limit reassignments across a function to keep intent clear.
Common mistake
Treating dynamic typing as license to reuse names for disparate purposes; prefer new variable names when types change meaningfully.

screens.title: Integers and Floating-point Numbers
screens.narratorSegment: Integers are whole numbers used for counts and indexes. Python integers have arbitrary precision, so they do not overflow like a fixed-size integer in some languages; this means you can safely work with large integers without unexpected wraparound. Floating-point numbers represent real numbers with a fractional component and are subject to typical precision limits of binary floating-point representation. This can produce results like 0.1 plus 0.2 not equaling an exact 0.3 due to rounding — a property shared with many languages. When you need exact decimal arithmetic for money, consider using specialized approaches, but for most beginner tasks the built-in float is appropriate. Use floor division when you need an integer quotient and true division when you want a precise fractional result. A small concrete example is splitting a bill: true division gives the precise share per person, while floor division gives whole units and may require handling a remainder. Understand operator behavior and convert types explicitly when combining integers and floats to ensure results match expectations. Integers and Floating-point Numbers means use integers for whole quantities and floats for fractional values; be aware of float precision and choose floor or true division depending on needed result.. In practical terms, whole numbers, precision, and what to expect when computing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Integers and Floating-point Numbers
Integers (int)
Whole numbers without a fractional part. Python integers grow to fit values instead of overflowing at a fixed size.
count = 42
big = 10 ** 20  # large integer handled safely
Use integers for counts, indexes, and cases where fractional parts are not meaningful.
Floating-point (float)
Numbers with fractional components. Floating-point arithmetic is approximate due to binary representation.
price = 19.99
share = 10 / 3  # true division, result is a float
quotient = 10 // 3  # floor division, integer result
For critical decimal precision, other approaches exist, but floats work well for many tasks. Choose division operator to match the result you need.
Concrete example
Splitting a 100 unit bill among 3 people: true division gives fractional shares; floor division gives whole units and requires handling the remainder.
Misconception
Expecting float arithmetic to be exact. Small rounding differences are normal and not bugs in your code logic.
Key takeaway
Pick int for discrete counts and float for fractional values; be deliberate with division operators and conversions.

screens.title: Strings and Booleans
screens.narratorSegment: Strings are sequences of characters enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes for multi-line text. Important to remember is that strings are immutable: operations like concatenation or slicing create new strings rather than changing existing ones. Use concatenation to join pieces, and slicing to extract substrings. Booleans represent truth values, typically produced by comparisons and logical operations. They are essential for control flow: conditions evaluate to a boolean that decides which path a program takes. A practical example is checking whether a user’s input matches a stored secret: the comparison yields a boolean used in an if statement to grant or deny access. A common beginner mistake is attempting arithmetic on string text without converting it to a numeric type first, or assuming a string can be modified in place. When building a greeting, read the name as text and treat it accordingly; when you need numeric computation, convert the text explicitly to an integer or float. This separation of concerns keeps logic clear and prevents runtime type errors. Strings and Booleans means strings are immutable sequences used for text; booleans capture true/false results and drive conditional behavior.. In practical terms, text handling, immutability, and truth values for control flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Strings and Booleans
Strings (str)
greeting = 'Hello'
name = "Alice"
message = greeting + ", " + name
snippet = message[0:5]  # slicing creates a new string
Strings are immutable; concatenation and slicing return new string values rather than altering existing ones.
Booleans (bool)
is_valid = (password == stored_password)
if is_valid:
    print("Access granted")
else:
    print("Access denied")
Comparisons produce booleans used to control flow. Combine booleans with logical operators to express complex conditions.
Concrete example
Check if a user’s favorite color equals a stored value and print a customized message when it does.
Common mistake
Trying to modify a string in place or using text where a number is required without converting it first.
Takeaway
Treat strings as immutable descriptors and booleans as the basis for decision-making in your programs.

screens.title: Input and Output: print and input
screens.narratorSegment: Output and input are how your program communicates with a user. The print function displays values to the console and can join multiple items with spaces when given several arguments. The input function shows a prompt and returns what the user types as text. A crucial detail is that input always returns text, so if you need to do arithmetic you must convert the text into a number using the language's numeric conversion functions. Forgetting this conversion results in type errors when you try to perform numeric operations. A concrete workflow: prompt the user for a birth year, convert it to an integer using the integer conversion function, compute age by subtracting from the current year, and then print a formatted greeting that mixes text and computed values. A misconception is thinking input returns the numeric type entered; it does not. Always validate or convert input explicitly, and consider handling conversion errors in more advanced programs. Input and Output: print and input means use the print function to show output and the input function to read text; convert input to numbers explicitly before arithmetic to avoid type errors.. In practical terms, displaying results and reading user-provided text safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Equality, inequality, and ordering operators let you ask questions like whether two values match or whether one is greater than another. These building blocks let you express practical checks: for example, verify that an entered year is in a reasonable range and that a favorite color matches one of several allowed options. fullNarratorScript:
You are transitioning from C to Python, and this shift is about expressing ideas with fewer low-level details. Python emphasizes readable layout: the structure of your code is visible in its indentation, so the way you space lines actually shapes program flow. That readability makes it easier to prototype solutions and collaborate. In this chapter you will learn how to write small Python programs using consistent indentation and comments, how variables receive types dynamically, and how the core data types — integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans — behave. You will also use the print function to show results and the input function to gather user text, remembering that input always returns a string and often needs conversion for numeric work. Finally, you will practice arithmetic, comparison and logical operators to make decisions and compute values. A short hands-on greeter ties these pieces together: ask for a name and birth year, convert types, compute an age, and print a formatted greeting. Keep an eye out for two common pitfalls: mixing tabs and spaces, and forgetting to convert input before doing math. How might those errors affect a simple greeter program you write?

These objectives focus your practice so you develop reliable beginner skills. First, you will understand Python's guiding philosophy of readability and simplicity. That means appreciating how indentation, clear naming, and concise constructs help you and others read code the same way. Second, you will write basic Python programs that use consistent indentation, useful comments, and simple variable assignment. This skill matters because correct indentation is required syntax in Python, not optional formatting. Third, you will identify and use the four fundamental data types: integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans. You will learn their essential properties — for example that strings are immutable and input always arrives as text. Fourth, you will perform input and output with the print function and the input function, and you will convert input strings into numbers when necessary to avoid runtime type errors. Practicing these four objectives gives you a foundation for composing larger programs and avoiding the most common beginner mistakes.

These objectives focus on practice and avoiding common mistakes. First, you will apply arithmetic operators such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, true division and floor division, and exponentiation so you can compute values correctly. You will also practice comparison operators to form boolean expressions that drive decisions in your code. Second, you will learn logical operators — and, or, and not — to combine conditions safely. Third, you will practice safe type handling with dynamic typing: variables can change type at runtime, so you will learn patterns to avoid confusing reassignments and to keep code predictable. Fourth, you will diagnose two frequent runtime issues: forgetting to convert input strings to numbers before arithmetic, which raises type errors, and mixing tabs and spaces which raises indentation errors. Each objective will be practiced with a short code example so you can see the error and the correct fix immediately.

A short side-by-side example makes the differences clear and actionable. In C, you declare a main function, include headers, and use explicit types and semicolons; the structure is delimited with braces. In Python, a simple print function and a line of text are often enough; no semicolons or explicit function wrapper is required for a top-level script. The key takeaway is that Python removes ceremony so you can express ideas faster, but it enforces structure through consistent indentation rather than braces. Try to read both examples aloud: notice how Python’s indentation shows scope directly, while C’s braces separate structural markers from the code body. A common misconception is to think Python doesn’t enforce structure — it does, via whitespace. Another is to assume Python lacks performance or control compared to C; different trade-offs exist but both are useful tools. Finally, practice converting small C snippets into Python: remove the type declarations and braces, keep the algorithm and logic, and rely on the interpreter to manage memory details for you. Hello, World — C vs Python means c uses explicit types, semicolons, and braces while python uses indentation and dynamic typing to express the same logic more concisely.. In practical terms, contrast syntax, explicit types, and the role of indentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Indentation in Python is not cosmetic — it determines program structure. Where other languages use braces to delimit a block of code, Python increases indentation to start a block and reduces it to end one. The conventional standard is four spaces per level. A frequent beginner error is mixing tabs and spaces: this can raise an indentation error that stops your program. To avoid this, configure your editor to insert spaces for tabs, and be consistent across the entire file. Consider a simple conditional: when a condition holds, the indented lines that follow are executed. If you accidentally align a line incorrectly, the interpreter will either treat it as outside the block or raise an error. A helpful mental model is thinking of indentation as a stack of nested scopes: each indentation level pushes a new scope, and dedenting pops it. Practice by reading samples and re-indenting with a consistent width; that practice will make reading and debugging faster. Finally, remember that comments do not affect indentation but must be aligned properly if they appear inside a block. Indentation and Block Structure means use consistent indentation (four spaces recommended); python uses indentation to mark blocks and mixing tabs with spaces causes syntax errors.. In practical terms, why whitespace defines control flow in python. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comments are written with the hash symbol and anything after that symbol on a line is ignored by the interpreter; use them to explain intent, not restate the code. Variable assignment in Python does not declare a type explicitly — the interpreter infers a variable’s type from its value when you assign it. For example, assigning ten sets the variable to an integer; later assigning a string replaces that value and type. This flexibility is powerful for quick experimentation but can also hide bugs if you accidentally reuse a name for a different kind of value. A concrete pattern is to keep variable names descriptive and consistent in use: use a name as a number holder or a text holder, not both. In the code panel you will see examples that show assignment, comments, and a reassignment that changes type. Notice the recommended habit: avoid reassigning wildly different types to the same name in a single scope. Also, prefer short comments that explain why a block exists rather than what each line does. Comments, Variables, and Dynamic Typing means use clear names and consistent uses for variables; dynamic typing helps speed development but requires disciplined naming to avoid confusion.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Integers are whole numbers used for counts and indexes. Python integers have arbitrary precision, so they do not overflow like a fixed-size integer in some languages; this means you can safely work with large integers without unexpected wraparound. Floating-point numbers represent real numbers with a fractional component and are subject to typical precision limits of binary floating-point representation. This can produce results like 0.1 plus 0.2 not equaling an exact 0.3 due to rounding — a property shared with many languages. When you need exact decimal arithmetic for money, consider using specialized approaches, but for most beginner tasks the built-in float is appropriate. Use floor division when you need an integer quotient and true division when you want a precise fractional result. A small concrete example is splitting a bill: true division gives the precise share per person, while floor division gives whole units and may require handling a remainder. Understand operator behavior and convert types explicitly when combining integers and floats to ensure results match expectations. Integers and Floating-point Numbers means use integers for whole quantities and floats for fractional values; be aware of float precision and choose floor or true division depending on needed result.. In practical terms, whole numbers, precision, and what to expect when computing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Strings are sequences of characters enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes for multi-line text. Important to remember is that strings are immutable: operations like concatenation or slicing create new strings rather than changing existing ones. Use concatenation to join pieces, and slicing to extract substrings. Booleans represent truth values, typically produced by comparisons and logical operations. They are essential for control flow: conditions evaluate to a boolean that decides which path a program takes. A practical example is checking whether a user’s input matches a stored secret: the comparison yields a boolean used in an if statement to grant or deny access. A common beginner mistake is attempting arithmetic on string text without converting it to a numeric type first, or assuming a string can be modified in place. When building a greeting, read the name as text and treat it accordingly; when you need numeric computation, convert the text explicitly to an integer or float. This separation of concerns keeps logic clear and prevents runtime type errors. Strings and Booleans means strings are immutable sequences used for text; booleans capture true/false results and drive conditional behavior.. In practical terms, text handling, immutability, and truth values for control flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Output and input are how your program communicates with a user. The print function displays values to the console and can join multiple items with spaces when given several arguments. The input function shows a prompt and returns what the user types as text. A crucial detail is that input always returns text, so if you need to do arithmetic you must convert the text into a number using the language's numeric conversion functions. Forgetting this conversion results in type errors when you try to perform numeric operations. A concrete workflow: prompt the user for a birth year, convert it to an integer using the integer conversion function, compute age by subtracting from the current year, and then print a formatted greeting that mixes text and computed values. A misconception is thinking input returns the numeric type entered; it does not. Always validate or convert input explicitly, and consider handling conversion errors in more advanced programs. Arithmetic operators let you perform basic calculations. The familiar operations addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division behave much like in mathematics. There are two division operators to be aware of: true division yields a floating-point result useful for averages and precise shares, while floor division returns an integer quotient useful for counts or when you intentionally want to discard the remainder. Modulo produces the remainder of a division and is handy for cyclic patterns, such as checking even or odd numbers. Exponentiation raises a value to a power. A concrete scenario: calculating a discount on a price involves multiplication and subtraction; splitting a bill among a group uses true division for equal shares. A common misconception is using floor division when you expect fractional results; always choose the operator that matches the desired numeric type. Comparison operators test relationships between values and return boolean results used to guide control flow. Equality, inequality, and ordering operators let you ask questions like whether two values match or whether one is greater than another. Logical operators combine these boolean results: and requires both conditions to hold, or requires at least one, and not negates a boolean. These building blocks let you express practical checks: for example, verify that an entered year is in a reasonable range and that a favorite color matches one of several allowed options. A common misconception is thinking logical operators short-circuit only in rare cases; short-circuiting is a useful behavior you can rely on to avoid unnecessary computation. Also use parentheses to combine comparisons clearly. Keep three quick rules in mind as you code. First, use consistent indentation; Python requires it to determine scope.
